# Explanation and prediction {#sec-explanation-prediction}

In 2017, a group of researchers issued an unusual challenge. The Fragile Families study had followed thousands of American children born around 2000, interviewing their families at birth and at ages one, three, five, and nine: nearly 13,000 variables per family, feeding a literature of over 750 published articles. The challenge: using everything measured through age nine, predict six outcomes at age fifteen, among them the child's grade point average and whether the family would be evicted. One hundred sixty teams tried, wielding every method from linear regression to deep learning, scored on families they had never seen. The best predictions were poor. For the two easiest outcomes the best team explained roughly 20% of the variance; for the other four, between 3% and 6%. A benchmark regression using just four variables chosen by a domain expert came embarrassingly close to the winners [@salganik2020].

Sit with the discomfort for a moment. Hundreds of papers had "explained" these children's development, and the same data could not *predict* their lives much better than guessing the average. Something is off in how we think about understanding, and this chapter locates it. The previous four chapters were about models whose parameters we interpret: effects, mechanisms, variance components. The coming chapters are about models built to predict, whose parameters may interest nobody. This chapter is the hinge. It asks what prediction is, what it is for, and what it has to do with explanation, and it can be read with a cup of coffee, since it contains almost no formulas at all.

## Prediction as a statement about unseen data

A prediction is a statement about data you have not seen. The data may lie in the future, but need not: predicting the outcomes of last year's held-back patients, whose files you never opened, is prediction in every sense that matters. What matters is that the model committed itself before the answer was known.

Science has always used prediction in this sense as its court of appeal. A theory implies statements about observations; the observations arrive; the theory survives or does not. You have already done this, in @sec-theory-to-glm, perhaps without noticing. A path model *implies* correlations, via the tracing rules, and the chi-square test asked whether the observed correlations obeyed. Every claim of absence was a commitment about data not yet consulted. In this sense, testing an explanation and checking a prediction are the same act.

Aggregate models make the same move at larger scale. The SIR model of epidemics [@kermack1927] divides a population into susceptible, infected, and recovered persons, and predicts a characteristic rise-peak-decline wave; real epidemics follow it roughly and depart from it instructively, and each departure (superspreading, waning immunity, behavior change) forced a better model. The DeGroot model of opinion dynamics [@degroot1974] predicts that people who keep averaging their opinions with their neighbors' will converge to consensus. Look around: no consensus. The model, taken literally, is false, and its failure is informative, since whatever blocks consensus (stubbornness, homophily) is exactly what a better theory must contain. Sociologists in the tradition of @coleman1990 and methodologists like @kkv1994 treat such observable implications as the currency of social theory: a theory that implies nothing checkable buys nothing.

There is a catch, and psychology spent a decade learning it. A verbal theory usually implies far less than its authors think, and testing "the theory predicts a difference in the expected direction" is a feeble hurdle; almost any theory clears it [@yarkoni2022]. Meehl's old complaint applies: predicting *that* it will rain in April is nothing, predicting how many millimeters on which days is science. One diagnosis of the replication crisis is exactly this mismatch between sweeping verbal claims and the timid statistical statements offered as their tests. Demanding real predictive performance, on data the model has not seen, is a discipline that verbal theorizing cannot fake.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 5.1"}
For each claim, state one concrete prediction it makes about unseen data, and one observation that would embarrass it. (a) The DeGroot model of opinion dynamics. (b) The mediation model of @sec-identification with no direct effect ($X \to M \to Y$ only). (c) "Vocational education helps early careers but hurts late ones" [@forster2016].
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 5.1"}
(a) Repeatedly interacting groups should drift toward agreement; stable long-run polarization in such groups embarrasses it. (b) The implied correlation restriction $\rho_{XY} = \rho_{XM}\rho_{MY}$ in fresh data; a clearly larger $\rho_{XY}$ embarrasses the exclusion. (c) In a new cohort, the employment gap between vocational and general graduates should be positive at labor-market entry and turn negative around mid-career; a gap that stays flat or grows with age embarrasses the reversal claim. In each case the theory earns credit only in proportion to how easily it could have failed.
:::

## Prediction in its own right

The second meaning of prediction needs no theory at all: sometimes an uncertain forecast is simply better than none, because a decision is waiting. Economists put the distinction in a picture worth keeping [@kleinberg2015]. Deciding whether to carry an umbrella requires only a forecast of rain: the umbrella does not change the weather. Deciding whether to perform a rain dance requires a causal claim: the dance pays only if it makes rain. Umbrella problems are everywhere once you look. Which arriving patients should be fast-tracked? Which defendants will appear for trial? Which households should an anti-poverty program visit first? In each case the decision needs to know who, and does not need to know why.

For most of the twentieth century, mainstream statistics in the social and health sciences treated such problems as beneath it. @breiman2001 called out the split in a paper that has aged embarrassingly well. Statistics, he wrote, contains two cultures. The data-modeling culture, which he estimated at 98% of statisticians, assumes a stochastic model and interprets its parameters, validating by goodness of fit. The algorithmic-modeling culture, his 2%, treats nature's mechanism as unknown, seeks any function that predicts well, and validates on held-out data. His warning to the 98% was blunt: conclusions from a fitted model are about the model's mechanism, and "if the model is a poor emulation of nature, the conclusions may be wrong". Twenty years later his 2% runs the technology sector, and this book's later chapters teach its methods.

Why would a model built without regard for truth predict better than a model built to be true? @shmueli2010 gives the clean answer: prediction error has two parts, error from bias (the model is wrong) and error from variance (the estimates are noisy), and a deliberately simplified, "wrong" model often wins by trading a little bias for a lot of variance. The full machinery of that trade-off is the next chapter's subject. For now, the moral: explaining well and predicting well are different objectives, optimized by different models, and neither can be read off from the other.

The habit of checking prediction pays off even inside ordinary explanatory research, which is the pragmatist's case made by @verhagen2022. Prediction is cheap: any fitted model, including the humble regressions of @sec-theory-to-glm, can be asked to predict, yet in six flagship journals of economics, sociology, and political science, fewer than 5% of abstracts even mention it. He calls the missing ingredient predictive consciousness: knowing whether your celebrated model captures 50% of the outcome's variation or 0.1%. It can be either, at the same $p$-value. Checking per group is more revealing still. A famous mortgage-discrimination analysis fits White applicants well and non-White applicants far worse, a fact invisible in its coefficient table and consequential for every conclusion drawn from it. And @yarkoni2017 close the circle with an unsettling identity: $p$-hacking, the fishing of @sec-rq-to-interpretation, is just overfitting performed by hand, "procedural overfitting". The machine learner's remedies, holding out data, penalizing flexibility, insisting on out-of-sample performance, are safeguards for explainers too.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 5.2"}
Classify each problem as umbrella (pure prediction suffices), rain dance (a causal claim is required), or a mix, and defend your answer in a sentence: (a) flagging which ICU patients are at high risk of deterioration tonight; (b) deciding whether to lower class sizes to raise test scores; (c) choosing which unemployed job-seekers get an intensive coaching program; (d) an insurer setting premiums from predicted health costs.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 5.2"}
(a) Umbrella: the alert changes staffing, not the patient's underlying risk; accuracy is what matters. (b) Rain dance: the policy *is* an intervention, so only the causal effect of class size justifies it. (c) A mix, and the interesting case: targeting needs prediction (who will stay unemployed?) but the program's value needs a causal effect (whom does coaching help?), and the highest-risk people need not be the most helped. (d) Umbrella for pricing accuracy, though the moment premiums change behavior, or encode discrimination, causal and ethical questions return through the back door.
:::

## The bitter lesson: language as the extreme case

If you want to see the algorithmic culture's wager pushed to its limit, look at language. For decades, the path to language technology was assumed to run through understanding: formal grammars and hand-built linguistic knowledge. A rival tradition, from the earliest corpus statisticians to the French data-analysis school of Jean-Paul Benzécri, treated language as data for counting rather than a system to axiomatize, and was long dismissed as shallow: surely you need to know *why* a sentence means what it means before a machine can use it. The verdict came in stages. In the 1970s, statistical models beat linguistically informed systems at speech recognition; over the decades that pattern repeated until @sutton2019 distilled it into the "bitter lesson" of seventy years of artificial intelligence: general methods that leverage computation and data eventually beat methods built on human domain knowledge, and the builders' bitterness is part of the story. Large language models are the current endpoint. Their training objective is pure prediction, the next word, with no explanatory ambition whatsoever, and yet they translate, summarize, diagnose, and tutor.

What does the extreme case offer social and health science, beyond a moral? Quite concrete tools, with quite concrete caveats. As *measurement instruments*, language models annotate text (stance, emotion, frames) at a quality approaching trained human coders on many tasks, though unevenly, which argues for using them as one coder on a human team rather than as an oracle [@ziems2024]. As *simulated participants*, they are startling and suspect at once: one large evaluation by Hewitt and colleagues, reported in a position paper reviewing the method, found a model predicting most of the variation in average treatment effects across dozens of preregistered experiments [@anthis2025], yet the same systems compress the variance of human opinion, misrepresent minorities, and may simply be remembering the studies they were trained on [@bail2024; @grossmann2023]. As *agents*, they revive agent-based modeling with actors that talk. The prudent summary: a purely predictive model of human text is a genuinely new scientific instrument, and every use of it re-raises this book's oldest question, namely what assumptions connect this instrument's output to the quantity we care about.

## Two mass collaborations

The Fragile Families Challenge that opened this chapter deserves a closer look, alongside its European successor, because together they are the cleanest measurements we have of how predictable individual lives are.

**The Fragile Families Challenge** [@salganik2020] borrowed machine learning's "common task method": one dataset, one holdout, one metric, many independent teams, so that failure cannot be blamed on any single researcher's skill. The material was rich by any social-science standard: 4,242 families, 12,942 variables spanning birth through age nine, purpose-built survey data rather than found data. Performance was scored as $R^2$ on held-out families, relative to simply predicting the average. The results, once more, with the numbers in view: the best submissions reached about 0.23 for material hardship and 0.19 for GPA, and 0.03 to 0.06 for grit, eviction, caregiver layoff, and job training. The four-variable expert benchmark was "only slightly worse than the most accurate submission". Two further findings sharpen the picture. The 160 teams' predictions, for all their methodological diversity, agreed with each other far more than any of them agreed with reality; and prediction error concentrated in particular *families*, not particular methods. The authors draw the conclusion carefully: the results "suggest practical limits to the predictability of life outcomes in some settings", and policymakers buying predictive tools for child protection or criminal justice should ask for exactly this kind of evidence before believing vendor accuracy claims.

**PreFer** [@sivak2024] is the designed follow-up, and its design shows a field learning. The task: predict which Dutch residents aged 18 to 45 will have a child in 2021 through 2023, from data through 2020. One outcome, well theorized, with a deliberately short three-year horizon. Two data sources compete. The LISS panel is "wide" in variables: over 30,000, including stated fertility intentions, the kind of subjective variable registers never contain, but with roughly 1,400 outcome-labeled cases. The Dutch population registers are "long" in cases: millions, 1995 through 2023, even the full kinship network, but limited to objective variables. The headline metric is F1, which balances precision and recall on the positive class, chosen because with about one in five positives, raw accuracy flatters models that predict "no child" for everyone. Teams submit runnable methods rather than predictions, fixing a reproducibility weakness the Fragile Families organizers discovered in their own archive. Above all, PreFer converts the earlier puzzle into a decomposition: if prediction fails on the survey but succeeds on the registers, the bottleneck was sample size; if the reverse, the subjective variables were the treasure; if both fail, the unpredictability starts to look like a property of lives rather than of datasets.^[The benchmark paper describes the challenge design; the challenge itself ran in 2024, and its results are reported separately by the organizers (see stulp.gmw.rug.nl/prefer). The joint lesson of this literature so far is consistent: predicting individual life outcomes is far harder than our explanatory confidence suggested.]

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 5.3"}
(a) In the Fragile Families Challenge, why does the common task method make "low predictability" a conclusion about the phenomenon rather than about the researchers? (b) The best GPA model reached $R^2 \approx 0.19$ against a mean-prediction baseline. A press release announces: "algorithm predicts children's school success". Write the two-sentence correction. (c) Explain why PreFer's organizers chose F1 rather than accuracy, using the base rates given above.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 5.3"}
(a) One hundred sixty independent teams with free choice of methods all faced the same holdout and the same metric; when the best of them barely beats a four-variable regression, "a better analyst would have done better" loses its plausibility, which was the design's purpose. (b) "The best of 160 competing models explained about a fifth of the variation in GPA, leaving four fifths unexplained; it beat a four-variable regression by a few points. Individual children's outcomes remained largely unpredictable from thirteen thousand variables." (c) With roughly 15 to 22% positives, predicting "no child" for everyone scores about 80% accuracy while identifying no one; F1, which balances precision and recall on the positive class, gives such a model the zero it deserves.
:::

## Pendulums: successes and failures

Fields swing between explanation and prediction, and the swings are instructive.

Macroeconomics swung twice. In the 1970s, its large "structural" models, hundreds of equations of interpretable theory, predicted poorly, and @sims1980 argued for replacing them with frankly atheoretical time-series models that simply let recent data forecast the near future. The forecasting improved; the approach earned Sims a Nobel prize in 2011. And then the pendulum returned: for questions about *policy*, rain-dance questions, forecasting models are silent by construction, and the following generation of economists rebuilt causal credibility with the designs and instruments of chapters 1 and 3, work honored with its own Nobel a decade later. Both swings were rational. The field learned which of its questions were umbrella questions and which were not.

Prediction has its cautionary tales too. Google Flu Trends estimated influenza incidence from search queries, faster than the official surveillance it aimed to complement, and for a while it worked; then it drifted, at one point overestimating flu prevalence by a factor of two, partly because the search engine and its users kept changing under the model [@lazer2014]. The failure is the mirror image of the Fragile Families lesson: an impressive fit on the past is a statement about the past, and a predictive model deployed in a changing world quietly becomes a model of a world that no longer exists. Meanwhile the quiet successes accumulate without headlines: clinical risk scores triage chest pain, predicted readmission risks schedule follow-up calls, and no one demands that these models explain anything, only that they keep being right.

## What to carry forward

Three ideas from this chapter travel into the machine learning chapters. Prediction is a statement about unseen data, so evaluation always requires data the model has not touched; how to arrange that, and how badly things go when you cheat, is the next chapter's subject under the names overfitting and cross-validation. A wrong model can predict better than the true one, which stops being a paradox once error is split into bias and variance. And the chain of @sec-rq-to-interpretation never went away: a predictive model answers its question under assumptions, chiefly that the future resembles the training data, and Google Flu shows what their violation looks like. The tools change in the next chapter. The five questions do not.

## Test yourself {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 5.A"}
A researcher has panel data on adolescents: social media use, sleep, exercise, parental monitoring, and depressive symptoms, over four years. Two goals are on the table. Goal 1: estimate the effect of social media use on depressive symptoms, for policy advice. Goal 2: flag adolescents at high risk of developing symptoms next year, so the school counselor can reach out.

(a) For each goal, which variables belong in the model, and by what criterion?
(b) For each goal, what is the appropriate way to judge whether the model is good?
(c) The Goal 2 model puts large weight on parental monitoring. A journalist concludes that monitoring causes depression. Explain the error, and what would go wrong if a school acted on it.
(d) Conversely, suppose the researcher uses only the variables with credible causal effects for Goal 2's forecasting task. What is sacrificed, and why?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 5.A"}
(a) Goal 1: variables chosen by the causal logic of chapters 1 and 3: confounders of use and symptoms must enter, mediators must stay out of the total-effect equation, and instruments or designs must carry the assumptions. Goal 2: anything measurable in advance that improves held-out prediction, including proxies with no causal standing. (b) Goal 1: by the credibility of the design and assumptions, plus uncertainty of the estimate; fit alone proves little. Goal 2: by predictive performance on held-out adolescents, with a metric suited to the base rate and to the costs of misses versus false alarms. (c) Predictors earn their weights by association, and monitoring may be a marker of parents already worried about a struggling child; acting on it causally (discouraging monitoring) could remove a response to risk rather than a cause of it, the umbrella-rain-dance confusion in the wild. (d) Predictive accuracy: causal variables are often few, weak, or hard to measure early, while non-causal markers carry real signal; a forecaster restricted to causes is a worse forecaster, which is Breiman's point in one sentence.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 5.B"}
A team proposes to use a language model to code 40,000 open-ended survey answers about vaccine hesitancy into five categories, replacing two student coders.

(a) Describe a validation design that would justify the substitution, including what quantity you would compute.
(b) Name two failure modes specific to language models that your design should probe, and how.
(c) The model classifies answers written in regional dialect noticeably worse. Which concept from this chapter (and from @sec-rq-to-interpretation) does this instantiate, and what would you do?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 5.B"}
(a) Have the human coders label a random subsample (stratified over categories and respondent groups); compare model and human labels via agreement statistics such as Cohen's kappa, benchmarked against the two humans' agreement with each other; only substitute if model-human agreement approaches human-human agreement, and keep humans on a continuing audit sample. (b) Training-data contamination and drift: probe by testing on newly written answers the model cannot have seen. Systematic skew, such as sycophantic or majority-flavored readings of ambiguous answers: probe by comparing error rates across answer types and demographic groups. (c) Differential measurement quality, a construct-validity threat, and a violation of the assumption that the instrument works equally well across units; remedies include dialect-specific validation, human coding for the affected group, or adjusting analyses for known error rates.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 5.C"}
"Since the best Fragile Families models explained only 20% of GPA variance, social science has learned nothing about child development." Write a short assessment (at most 200 words) that engages the strongest version of both sides.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 5.C"}
A model answer engages both directions. For the provocation: if understanding is measured by out-of-sample prediction, the result is damning, since 750 papers' worth of variables barely beat four chosen by hand, and the shortfall was no one team's fault by design. Against it: explanation and prediction are different targets; a modest average causal effect can be real, replicable, and policy-relevant while individual outcomes stay dominated by idiosyncratic events, so low individual predictability does not refute the causal knowledge. The strong synthesis notes what the challenge actually adds: a measured ceiling, so far unexplained, which theories of development must now themselves explain; a warning for anyone deploying individual-level risk prediction in policy; and a template, extended by PreFer, for finding out whether the ceiling reflects data limits or genuine randomness in lives. "Nothing" overclaims; "business as usual" underclaims; the defensible position is that social science learned something painful and useful about the kind of knowledge it has.
:::
